title: Full Planning or Day-of Coordination in Punta Cana?
seoTitle: Full Planning or Day-of Coordination in Punta Cana?
description: Choose full planning or wedding-day coordination in Punta Cana by comparing decisions, supplier responsibilities, handover and event coverage.
directAnswer: Choose full planning when you need help shaping the wedding, selecting venues and suppliers, and managing decisions over time. Choose wedding-day coordination when the main bookings and design are settled and you need a professional to review and execute the plan. The contract must define preparation, event dates, responsibilities and exclusions; service labels alone are not enough.

sections.heading: Start with the work remaining, not the package name
paragraphs: Full planning and day-of coordination solve different problems. Planning develops decisions into a workable event: which venue fits, what each supplier delivers, how the budget is allocated and when approvals are needed. Coordination brings confirmed commitments together so people can execute them in the correct order. The services overlap in places, but they begin from different levels of readiness.

Make a list of your remaining decisions before requesting quotes. Separate choices that require research from tasks that require confirmation. Selecting a venue is research; checking a booked venue's access time is confirmation. Designing a reception is development; distributing an approved seating plan is coordination. If most tasks remain in the first category, describe them honestly rather than assuming they fit a lower-priced service.

A wedding in Punta Cana also involves travel and communication across locations. Explain where you live, who can answer questions during local working hours and whether guests are using several hotels. These circumstances do not automatically require full planning, but they affect the amount of work someone must own. The useful question is who will perform each task, with enough time and information to do it.

sections.heading: Understand the decisions covered by full planning
paragraphs: Ask a full planner to describe their deliverables at each stage. Early work might include translating your priorities into a brief, researching suitable venues and comparing supplier proposals. Later work should explain how approved decisions become a budget, timeline and operational plan. The contract should identify the actual services rather than imply that the word full covers every request.

Clarify your own role in approvals. A planner can research and organize options, but the couple needs a clear process for authorizing purchases, choosing suppliers and accepting changes. Agree who can make decisions if the partners are unavailable and what requires both partners' approval. Without that process, even a well-prepared recommendation can remain blocked until a supplier's availability changes.

Ask how the team records decisions and tracks outstanding work. A simple shared list can be sufficient when it identifies the owner, deadline, dependency and status. What matters is that an unanswered menu question does not disappear while a décor proposal moves ahead. Full planning is especially useful when you want professional support building that decision process, not only attending the celebration.

sections.heading: Understand what day-of coordination needs before the wedding
paragraphs: Day-of coordination cannot be defined usefully as a person arriving with no knowledge of the event. Ask when the coordinator reviews the venue, supplier agreements and timeline. Explain which decisions are complete and which remain open. A professional needs to identify gaps, confirm contacts and establish a realistic sequence before taking responsibility for wedding-day communication.

Prepare the approved supplier list, contracts, payment status, layouts, guest count and event schedule. Include details that change delivery: access restrictions, unloading instructions, dietary requests, ceremony participants and any agreed weather alternative. Mark tentative items explicitly. A coordinator cannot safely treat an inspiration board, an unsigned quote and an approved production order as equivalent instructions.

Ask what happens when the review uncovers missing planning. An unbooked photographer or an undecided dinner format may require additional work beyond coordination. Agree whether the couple will complete it, a supplier will resolve it or the coordinator will quote an expanded scope. Choosing a service realistically at the start is easier than discovering close to the wedding that nobody owns a major decision.

sections.heading: Compare published services without generalizing their terms
paragraphs: Sertuin Events' service page, consulted November 18, 2026, describes standard full planning at USD2,500 and wedding-day coordination at USD1,200. Full planning covers the planning process and wedding-day management within the agreed scope. Day coordination includes review beginning when contracted, and the published service excludes the rehearsal. Third-party purchases remain separate. These are company offers, not universal Punta Cana definitions or average market fees.

Use the published distinction to request a personal proposal. Confirm the exact event date, activities covered, team responsibilities and payment terms. A fee comparison becomes meaningful only when both offers cover the work you actually need. Do not infer that a higher price includes travel bookings, extra event days or a religious ceremony specialist unless those services are identified.

Other providers may use different labels or organize their work differently. Some may offer a partial-planning arrangement, but availability and scope must be confirmed directly. Compare deliverables instead of trying to force each offer into a familiar name. You should be able to explain what the professional starts with, what they produce and what remains your responsibility.

sections.heading: Map the boundary between your planner and the venue team
paragraphs: A resort or private venue can have an events contact with important responsibilities for its own spaces and services. Ask what that person manages and which tasks belong elsewhere. Venue operations, external suppliers, guest transport and family instructions should not depend on assumptions about who is the overall point of contact. More than one professional can be involved without duplicating the same job.

Create a responsibility list for major moments: supplier arrival, ceremony setup, guest seating, dinner service, speeches, music cues and final collection of personal items. For each moment, name the person who executes it and the person who checks that it is ready. A venue team may manage food service while an independent coordinator aligns the speeches with the kitchen; both roles can be necessary.

Agree how instructions flow. Suppliers should know whose timeline is current and whom to call if something changes. Avoid sending separate versions from the couple, hotel and coordinator without reconciliation. The goal is not to replace a venue's procedures, but to connect the people delivering different parts of the wedding through one approved plan.

sections.heading: Treat guest logistics as a defined scope
paragraphs: Guest logistics can mean anything from sharing hotel information to coordinating multiple transport departures. Write down the work you expect. Is someone creating travel guidance, collecting arrival information, helping compare accommodation or communicating with a transport provider? Does that person book and pay for travel, or only coordinate information? Those activities should not be confused.

Choose one channel for guest questions and decide who maintains it. Share practical details such as event locations, transport instructions and the deadline for providing dietary information. Avoid collecting sensitive information without a clear need. For a simple group, a concise guest guide and named contact may be enough; a dispersed group may need a more detailed arrival and movement plan.

Ask how last-minute changes will be handled. If a guest misses an agreed shuttle, who contacts the transport company and who approves an additional cost? If a hotel changes a pickup point, who updates guests? Day coordination may cover wedding-day movements while earlier travel arrangements remain elsewhere. Full planning also needs explicit boundaries; it does not automatically become a travel agency service.

sections.heading: Include cultural requirements without assigning ritual authority incorrectly
paragraphs: Describe cultural, religious and family expectations early enough to assess the work. A ceremony may require specific participants, objects, food arrangements or a sequence that affects the event schedule. Ask the appropriate cultural or religious authority to define the ritual requirements, then have the planner coordinate the logistics with that person. Operational coordination should support those instructions rather than invent them.

For celebrations on several days, list each event, location, supplier and guest group. A service covering the wedding day does not automatically cover a welcome gathering or another ceremony. Likewise, full planning for one event should not be interpreted as unlimited attendance across a week. Ask for separate coverage where necessary and identify handovers between teams.

Create a clear route for family requests. A helpful relative may propose a timing change that affects photography, catering and transport. Decide which family representative can clarify traditions and which person can authorize a change to the agreed plan. This respects the meaning of the celebration while allowing suppliers to work from consistent instructions.

sections.heading: Compare total workload and fees honestly
paragraphs: A lower professional fee does not mean the remaining work disappears. If you choose coordination, identify the research, supplier selection and approvals you will complete yourselves. Consider whether you have the time, access to information and interest to do that work. You do not need to enjoy every task, but you should know who will complete it before its deadline.

Separate the planning fee from event purchases. Venue rental, catering, decoration, photography and transport may be charged by other providers. Ask how extra events, changed scope or additional services affect the professional's fee. Obtain a written change process so a new request produces a clear scope and price before work is authorized.

Avoid hypothetical savings claims. A planner may identify options and help compare proposals, but no responsible budget should assume that unspecified discounts will pay the fee. Assess the service through the work it performs and the support you value. A transparent proposal lets you compare that value with the practical work and responsibility you retain.

sections.heading: Prepare a handover that another professional can actually use
paragraphs: Start with a concise event summary: who is attending, where each activity occurs, the approved timetable and the latest decisions. Attach the signed contracts and confirmed supplier details. Record payment status without distributing unnecessary banking information. Include a list of unresolved items with named owners rather than leaving the coordinator to discover them through conflicting messages.

Review the timeline with suppliers whose tasks depend on one another. Photography needs to align with ceremony readiness; food service needs to know when guests will sit; transport needs to match event access. Build realistic transitions instead of placing every activity directly after the previous one. Ask the team to flag conflicts before the couple approves the final schedule.

Agree on the final version and change procedure. The coordinator should know who can authorize extra expenses and whom to contact if the couple wants to be unavailable during preparations. Provide a backup contact who understands the limits of that authority. A handover is complete when someone else can explain and run the plan, not merely when a folder has been shared.

sections.heading: Choose the service through a practical conversation
paragraphs: Consider a couple with no venue, a rough budget and several competing ideas. Their central need is developing and making decisions, so full planning is the relevant conversation. Consider another couple with signed suppliers, an approved design and a clear budget who wants professional management of the event. Their central need may be coordination, provided the review confirms that the plan is ready.

There are also mixed situations. You may have booked the venue but still need help sourcing most suppliers, or have designed the event but not organized guest movements. Describe that actual state. Ask the professional to identify work included, work excluded and any conditions before accepting responsibility. This is more useful than choosing a label simply because it sounds familiar.

Before signing, check that you can answer four questions: who develops unfinished decisions, who communicates with suppliers, who is present for each event and who approves changes. Ask for a written answer wherever responsibility is unclear. The appropriate service is the one that covers your real needs and leaves the remaining tasks with people who have agreed to do them.

faqs.question: Is day-of coordination really limited to work on that day?
faqs.answer: The event coverage and preparation period are separate questions. Ask when review begins and what documents must be ready. Sertuin Events states that its venue, supplier and timeline review starts when contracted, while its on-site service covers the wedding day and excludes the rehearsal. Confirm your exact scope in writing.

faqs.question: Do we need an independent coordinator if the venue has one?
faqs.answer: It depends on responsibilities. Ask the venue what it manages, then identify any work involving independent suppliers, guest movements or family communication that remains outside that service. If all needed work is clearly assigned, you can assess whether another professional adds useful coverage.

faqs.question: Does full planning mean we lose control of our choices?
faqs.answer: The approval process should preserve the couple's decisions. Agree who researches, recommends and authorizes each purchase, and how changes are recorded. Professional support can organize the choices while you retain the approvals defined in the contract.

faqs.question: Can coordination cover a welcome dinner or rehearsal?
faqs.answer: Only if those activities are included in the agreed scope. List each event and date when requesting a quote. Do not assume that wedding-day coverage extends to another day or that rehearsal attendance is automatic.

faqs.question: What if we already booked some suppliers?
faqs.answer: Share the contracts and explain the decisions still outstanding. A professional can assess whether the remaining work fits coordination or requires broader planning. Existing bookings are useful context, but their number alone does not establish that the full event is ready for handover.
